full_judgment:
This rule at the Instance of the pre-emptee is directed against the Judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Noakhali dated 8.6.79 in Misc. Appeal No. 78 1978 affirming those passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court Lakshmipur in Misc. Case No. 79 of 1966 and arises out of an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The opposite parties Nos. 1 to 11 who were pre-emptors filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the disputed land detailed in the schedule, by the original pre-emptee who was the father of the petitioners Nos. 1 and 4 here on obtaining a decree for Specific Performance of Control by a kabala dated 18.1.63 registered on 13.3.66. 

 2. The pre-emptors case was to the effect that they were co-sharers with regard to the disputed holding by prior purchase and came to know of the sale only for the first time on 3.4.66. They after taking certified copy of the kabala came to know of the sale definitely and thereafter depositing the consideration money along wish the statutory compensation filed the application for pre-emption on 16.5.66. They further contended that the opposite party No. 1 was a stranger to the holding. The application for pre-emption was contested by opposite parties Nos. 1 to 3 and 11 who contended, inter alit, that the petition was not maintainable in its present form and was barred by limitation and the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and was bad for defect of parties. They also denied the allegation and statements made in the application. They, however, claimed, that they too are co-sharers In the case holding and in case Pie petition for pre-emption is allowed, they are also entitled to rateable pre-emption according to their shares. 

 “For that the land in question being a part of a tenure (Sikkimi Maddya Satia) there was no right of pre-emption in respect thereof under the Bengal Tenancy Act and the transfer is dispute based on the agreement to sell dated 24 5 57 which was the date of transfer on the passing of the decree for specific performance of the contract for sale on 2. 1962 (though the kabala executed by the learned Munsif on 18.1.1963 was registered on 18.3.66) there did not arise any right of pre emption under section 96(1) of E.B. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1951, which was applied to the area by enforcing Part V of the said Act on 1.8.1963. So, the case was governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act and not the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the learned Courts below exercised Jurisdiction not vested in them by law in allowing the application for pre-emption as the land of a holding of a raiyat". 

 In elaborating his arguments Mr. Khondker submits that in vie v of the decree passed in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract, It will date back to the date of agreement since this transfer in dispute was based on an agreement to sell dated 24.5.57 and on that date the right of pre-emption under section 96 was not available. As such the case was governed by e. 2e (F) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. 

 He further submits that Part V of the State Acquisition Act came into force in the area on 1.8 63 and only on that date of coming Into force or this part, there shall be within that area only one class of agricultural tenant. Before that the Bengal Tenancy Act was in force and section 26 (F) B.T. Act did not apply to the class of holders of tenure, called "Sikkiml Maddya Satta tenure". 

 6. Mr. Khondker Mahbabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, on the other hand, submits that the right of pre-emption accrued from the date of registration r f the document and after its registration, it will take effect from the date of execution. He submits that the contract was dated 24.5.57 but since the specific performance was not effected a suit was brought by the opposite party No. 1 before the learned Munsif which was decreed on 7.2.62. Pursuant to the decree the Court executed the kabala for sale on 18.1.61 and the same was registered on 18.3 66. So on the date when the kabala was executed i.e. on 18.1.63 Part V of the Sate Acquisition Act came into force in the area In which the case land is situate and by the time, which the kabala was executed, the provisions of 26(F) B T. Act lost i's force and the matter was governed by section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. He further submits that the right of pre-emption accrued only on registration of the document and not earlier. Here the date of registration was 18.3.66 and on that date the Bengal Tenancy Act was not in existence and there was no existence of Sikkim, Maddya Satta. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, last paragraph, is to the following effect: 

 So a property can be transferred only by a conveyance and not by mere agreement between the parties. A contract for sale by itself does not create any interest or charge in the property. Law requires a conveyance for the purpose of transfer of title and this cannot be made by agreement. Of course, under the English Law, a purchaser, by virtue of contract of sale, becomes complete owner of the property from the date of contract but that principle of English Law has no application to a place where toe Transfer of Property Act is in force. In that view of the matter the contention of the learned Advocate of the pre-emptee petitioners that the transfer dates back to the date of agreement for sale cannot be accepted. Mr. Khondker in support of his arguments relied upon a decision reported In 16 D.L.R. (SC) page 706 but that case was with regard the put performance of contract. The facts and circumstances of that 16 D.L R. (SC) 706 case are completely different from the facts and circumstances of the present case and has no application here. In that case a suit for specific performance of contract was decreed on 3.11.51 and an appeal was preferred to the High Court against the decree which was dismissed on 6.2.58. The contract was entered into on 30.9 47 and some consideration passed. On 13.12.58 a portion of the land was compulsorily acquired by the Government and compensation for the acquired laud was assessed. The decree-holder applied for amendment of the decree for the purpose of getting the kabala in respect of the compensation money awarded by the Government and the Court accordingly directed that the defendant shall execute the kabala in respect of the award money as fixed by the Government On appeal a point was taken that the contract has become frustrated in respect of the land which was compulsorily acquired by the Government and could not be enforced to that extent. There it was held that in view of sections 12 & 14 of the Specific Relief Act there was no question of frustration of the contract, and it being clear that at least after the making of the decree, the land vested in the purchaser which tad already gone into his possession, the right to the compensation money for the land. lost by reasons of the acquisition by the Government, clearly vested in the purchaser who shall have exclusive claim to the compensation money. But here in the present case the contract as stated earlier was dated 4.5.57 and the decree was dated 7.2.62 and the date of execution of the kabala was dated 18.1.63. So the kabala being executed on 18.1.63 and the registration being completed on 18.3.63 the right to transfer accrued from the date of registration of the kabala dated 18.3.63 and that would be the date for determining the status of class of tenancy. In case of transfer, the Dalton which the transfer takes effect is the date of instrument and not the date of registration but in case of pre-emption the date of registration gives rise to the accrual of the right of pre-emption (17 D.L.R.(Dacca) 365 and 21 D. L. R. 599). So, in that view of the matter, right of pre-emption hiving accrued on 18.1.63 the contention of Mr. H. M. Khondker the learned advocate that the tenancy was governed by the provision of section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the nature of the Tenancy being Sikkimi Maddya Satta was not liable to pre-emption his no force. Registration of document having been completed in 1968, the tenancy would be governed by the law applicable at that time. By that time Part V of the State Acquisition Act has come into force and there existed only one class of holders of agricultural land. The tenancy was therefore governed by the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and section 96 was applicable to the facts and circumstances of the oats. No other point has been urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.
